Remember that marble is $\text{CaCO}_3$, a carbonate that reacts with acids, so look for the emission that can form acid rain.

walkthrough:
**What Is Marble and Why Does It Erode?**

Marble is mainly calcium carbonate, $\text{CaCO}_3$. Carbonates are attacked by acids, which dissolve them and release carbon dioxide.

Key reaction idea:
$$\text{CaCO}_3 + 2\text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{Ca}^{2+} + \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Which Engine Emission Forms Acid?**

In the very hot engine, nitrogen and oxygen from air react to form nitrogen oxides, $\text{NO}_x$. Nitrogen dioxide dissolves in rain to form nitric acid, a component of acid rain.

Acid formation:
$$2\text{NO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{HNO}_3 + \text{HNO}_2$$

**Link Acid Rain to Erosion**

That nitric acid, $\text{HNO}_3$, falls as acid rain onto statues and reacts with the $\text{CaCO}_3$. This slowly dissolves the surface, so the detail is eroded away.

options.A: Carbon monoxide, $\text{CO}$, is toxic because it binds to haemoglobin, but it is neutral and does not form an acid in rain. It therefore does not dissolve $\text{CaCO}_3$.
options.B: Nitrogen, $\text{N}_2$, makes up about 78% of clean air and is very unreactive under normal conditions. It does not form acid and does not attack marble.
options.C: Nitrogen dioxide, $\text{NO}_2$, is formed in the engine at high temperature and is oxidised in air. It dissolves in water to give nitric acid, $\text{HNO}_3$, which reacts with and erodes calcium carbonate marble.
options.D: Unburnt hydrocarbons contribute to photochemical smog and are pollutants, but they do not directly form strong acids that erode marble in the way nitrogen oxides do.
